title_original: A Look Inside the 2026 PhotoBook Awards Shortlist
excerpt_original: These 35 photobooks highlight excellence in publishing across a wide range of topics and photographic styles.

blocks.text: This year, Aperture received a record number of books from fifty-six countries around the world for the Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards, an annual celebration of the vibrant field of photobook publishing. Now in its fourteenth year, the awards recognize excellence in three major categories of photobook publishing: First PhotoBook, PhotoBook of the Year, and Photography Catalog of the Year.

In September, the shortlist jury met in New York for three concentrated days of review and deliberation by an international team which included Alejandro Cartagena, artist; Alexandra Cunningham Cameron, director of design, Judd Foundation; Michael Famighetti, editor in chief, Aperture; Anna Planas, artistic director, Paris Photo; and Anshika Varma, curator and founder, Offset Projects.

The shortlisted books will be exhibited at Paris Photo , open to the public from November 12 through November 15, followed by an international tour, including in Dublin at PhotoIreland, in December 2026, and other venues to be announced. Below is a look inside the thirty-five selected titles for the 2026 PhotoBook Awards shortlist. Stay tuned for the announcement of the winners, which will take place on Friday, November 13, at 3 p.m. (CET) at the Balcon de l’Horloge at the Grand Palais.
First PhotoBook

blocks.caption: Ivan Anisimov, from Pants on Top of Shoes , 2025 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Pants on Top of Shoes by Ivan Anisimov Kult Books, Stockholm. Design by Janne Riikonen

This book does exactly what its title promises: After moving to Tbilisi from his native Russia, Ivan Anisimov began photographing the feet of local passersby, struck by how their untailored trousers draped over their shoes. Focusing on bunched-up fabric and scuffed leather became a way for Anisimov to negotiate his sense of belonging in a new country governed by its own visual codes. Printed in black and white on uncoated paper, Pants on Top of Shoes has a quick, handheld quality that feels apt for photographs made in motion—what at first feels like a whimsical typology of trousers and shoes gradually becomes an inquiry into difference, sameness, and the politics of looking.

blocks.caption: Amparo Baquerizas, from Gauchito Querido , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Gauchito Querido by Amparo Baquerizas Editorial RM, México and Barcelona. Design by Amparo Baquerizas

Where is Gauchito Gil? This question lodged itself in Amparo Baquerizas’s mind following his return to Argentina after over a decade away. In his book Gauchito Querido , he boldly and playfully reconstructs a pilgrimage to Mercedes, Corrientes, the purported birthplace of the Argentine folk-saint Antonio Mamerto Gil Núñez, lovingly nicknamed “Gauchito,” or little Gaucho. Honing in on the color red, a staple of the saint’s garb, Gauchito Querido reconfigures the genre of the photo-road-trip using screenshots from Google Street View, testimonies from the followers of Gauchito, and scans of devotional paraphernalia encountered at the various altars and shrines the artist found on his journey. Baquerizas thoughtfully makes sure the reader doesn’t lose their way in their own journey through the book: red prayer ribbons affixed to the spine act as bookmarks in case one gets lost.

blocks.caption: Miranda Barnes, from Social Season , 2026 Courtesy the artist and MACK

blocks.text: Social Season by Miranda Barnes Important Flowers, London. Design by Anamaria Morris

Through photographs made at debutante balls in Detroit from 2022 to 2025, Miranda Barnes’s debut explores the history of Black cotillion culture. The debutante tradition—a coming-of-age rite once reserved for white European nobility—was reclaimed and integrated into the African American community in the wake of emancipation. Formal portraits of debutantes, backstage glimpses, and lively scenes of couples dancing are woven together in a dreamy sequence, punctuated with details of the material extravagance distinctive of the world of cotillion. The elegance and sensitivity with which Barnes makes photographs are echoed in the classic design of the book, creating a timeless document of a cultural experience grounded in its extensive history, vibrant present, and evolving future.

blocks.caption: Sara Bennett, from Looking Inside: Women with Life Sentences , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Looking Inside: Women with Life Sentences by Sara Bennett Kehrer Verlag, Heidelberg, Germany. Design by Teun van der Heijden and Heijdens Karwei

links.text: Looking Inside: Women with Life Sentences

blocks.text: Following a career as a public defender, Sara Bennett spent over a decade photographing women convicted of violent crimes. Looking Inside: Women with Life Sentences combines Bennett’s portraits of the women she met and collaborated with—spanning their lives inside prison walls to their reentry into the outside world—with personal ephemera like letters, polaroids, and drawings to weave a layered story of humanity. Each portrait is paired with a handwritten response to the question “When you see this photo . . . what does it make you think?” bearing witness to their experiences from within a cell to their reconciliation with feelings of regret and forgiveness. Shining a compassionate light on an often underrepresented population within the discourse surrounding mass incarceration, Bennett invites us to question the justice system as we know it.

blocks.caption: Nata Drachinskaya, from Binom , 2025 Courtesy BLOW UP PRESS

blocks.text: Binom by Nata Drachinskaya BLOW UP PRESS, Warsaw, and Rencontres d’Arles, France. Design by Nata Drachinskaya, Yumi Goto, Aneta Kowalczyk, and Jan Rosseel

Linguistics and mathematics have it that the binomial indicates a component or expression consisting of two semantically correlated parts, its meaning originally deriving from the Latin binomium—that which has two names. Binom by Nata Drachinskaya is an elaborate foray into the revelations and foreclosures involved in discovering that her own father essentially lived a secret and parallel life as a cryptographer. The book, which fuses two slipcases and two volumes, also attempts to fuse the two parts of her father’s life together. Yet the process is not so simple. Inside each volume, the reader’s attempts at learning are thwarted by partially uncut pages, photograph versos, and texts obfuscated by ephemera supposedly connected to her father’s activities.

blocks.caption: Franco Dupuy, Chapter 02. Park’s Public Restrooms , from Cruising Diaries , 2025 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Cruising Diaries by Franco Dupuy Set Margins, Eindhoven, Netherlands. Design by Furio and Santiago Bogani

Franco Dupuy combines diary and document in Cruising Diaries , guiding readers through the personal geographies of anonymous queer desire and pleasure. The Swiss-bound softcover volume is pocketbook sized, a compact form for black-and-white images that register the clandestine thrills and sultry intermissions of his nocturnal encounters. Dupuy’s own voice escorts us through spaces, strategies, and reflections on cruising in the textual interludes that accompany his photographs. An intelligently designed and gratifying combination of text and image, Cruising Diaries attempts to accrue a visual language for a practice that resists being seen.

blocks.caption: Jakob Ganslmeier and Ana Zibelnik, from If a Flower Bloomed in a Dark Room, Would You Trust It? , 2025 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: If a Flower Bloomed in a Dark Room, Would You Trust It? by Jakob Ganslmeier and Ana Zibelnik Spector Books, Leipzig, Germany. Design by Hamid Sallali

links.text: If a Flower Bloomed in a Dark Room, Would You Trust It?

blocks.text: If a Flower Bloomed in a Dark Room, Would You Trust It? serves up two mainstream social media trends—spiritual hustling and looksmaxxing—to the reader on opposite sides of a single book, and considers the dissemination of and entrapment by ideologies through the proliferation of images on social media platforms such as TikTok. Rephotographed phone screens rendered in black and white make “harmless” content melancholy and strange, while crowded, didactic diagrams map out lessons in visual literacy. Though the book presents two sides of a spinning coin that’s nearly impossible to ignore, it also reminds the reader, in its inclusion of smudges and fingerprints, of the sensorial subject on the other side of the screen who’s grasping for a way to live.

blocks.caption: Jesse Glazzard, from The Sound of Dirt and Beauty , 2026 Courtesy the artist and MACK

blocks.text: The Sound of Dirt and Beauty by Jesse Glazzard SPBH Editions, London. Design by Brian Paul Lamotte

links.text: The Sound of Dirt and Beauty

blocks.text: A raw, unfiltered testament to community and chosen family, Jesse Glazzard’s The Sound of Dirt and Beauty speaks to the lives of queer youth in the UK today. Echoing Glazzard’s previous self-published zines, the book is a screen-printed softcover with a sense of immediacy and openness. As Glazzard’s own transition unfolds throughout the book in a series of self-portraits, the reader becomes a witness to the accompanying moments of pain and pleasure depicted in portraits staged in homes and bedrooms and images of friends gathered in parks, presenting a record of embrace and communion.

blocks.caption: Ma Hailun, from Üruklyn , 2025 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Üruklyn by Ma Hailun Jiazazhi, Ningbo, China. Design by Studio Pianpian He and Max Harvey

The title of Üruklyn is a portmanteau of Brooklyn and Ürümqi , Hailun Ma’s hometown in Xinjiang—China’s westernmost region, home to 25 million people and more than forty ethnic groups, many of them Muslim majority. These include the Uyghurs, a predominantly Muslim Turkic people who have faced systematic persecution by the Chinese government, including mass detention, constraints on religious and cultural freedoms, and forced labor. After studying fashion photography in New York, Ma sought to explore the artistic potential of Xinjiang; the photographs in Üruklyn celebrate the everyday traditions and style of Uyghur teenagers, Kazakh cowboys, and other communities sidelined in mainstream depictions of the country. The book itself feels highly crafted, with a silkscreened cover, decorative inserts, and vibrant endpapers patterned after Uzbek textiles that ground the object in the visual textures of the region.

blocks.caption: Moeko Ishiguro, from Notation(s) , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Notation(s) by Moeko Ishiguro Self-published, Tokyo. Design by Moeko Ishiguro

Moeko Ishiguro’s self-published debut feels less like a book than an intricate sculpture, dispensing as it does with traditional pagination in favor of folds, overlaps, and shifting layers that must be physically negotiated by the reader. The photographs—wryly observed and uncannily seductive shots of concrete planters, litter, and other mundane phenomena—are revealed through a process of peeling back layers of paper, making each image appear discovered rather than simply turned to. Around the height and width of a smartphone, this book offers a brilliant alternative to passive scrolling, asking readers to spend time with images that refuse to surrender their core unknowability.

blocks.caption: Adél Koleszár, Grave , Veracruz, Mexico, 2018 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Only Have Faith ( Solamente Ten Fe ) by Adél Koleszár Art Paper Editions, Ghent, Belgium. Design by Jurgen Maelfeyt

links.text: Only Have Faith ( Solamente Ten Fe

blocks.text: Adél Koleszár’s Only Have Faith is a statement against the spectacle of violence commonly associated with Mexico’s drug trade and American intervention. The project closely follows the excavation of a mass grave in Veracruz, Mexico—the result of criminal organizations and complicit authorities forcibly disappearing citizens—and tells the story of Colectivo Solecito de Veracruz, a volunteer collective of women who continue to look for their disappeared loved ones. Photographs that extend to the edge of the page deeply immerse the reader in the world, while occasional text and image spreads allow space for their personal testimony to be heard.

blocks.caption: Jeremy Liebman, from Coincidence , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Coincidence by Jeremy Liebman Apartamento Publishing S.L., Barcelona. Design by Apartamento Studios and Laura Delgado

Coincidence is the story of three generations of Jeremy Liebman’s family across Dallas, Brooklyn, and the English shires. As Liebman’s father grapples with the ravages of Alzheimer’s, his daughter is learning to talk, and the book’s nimble pairings of high-contrast black-and-white images tease out the ironies of the situation, stringing together an ambiguous narrative where first memories are mixed with last ones. The book’s relatively compact scale encourages a more private encounter—an apt choice for these photographs, which walk a deft line between nostalgic family album and a father’s and son’s acts of creative, uncompromising witness.

blocks.caption: Augustin Lignier, from Turning Point , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Turning Point by Augustin Lignier Art Paper Editions, Ghent, Belgium. Design by Jurgen Maelfeyt

Turning Point features sixty out of six thousand images taken of and by Augustin Lignier as he jumps up and spins in a circle, attempting to capture himself landing face forward toward the camera’s shutter. With only one simple task, he questions what it means to make the “perfect” photograph—if it exists—through the mundane, repetitive nature of humanity. The book is spiral bound, with each black-and-white exposure accompanied by reams of metadata documenting Lignier’s obsessive pursuit of the “decisive” leap. These choices lend Turning Point the look and feel of a proper scientific research project, amplifying the absurdity of his quest and, by extension, our own absurd search for total fulfillment.

blocks.caption: João Linneu, from JJ VFF VV , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: JJ VFF VV by João Linneu Void, Athens. Design by Void

In JJ VFF VV , João Linneu portrays his partner Fernanda Fajardo navigating the challenging pregnancy and premature birth of their first child, Valentín, in 2014. Linneu’s tender yet steady scenes of a bedroom, bathroom, and hospital ward are interspersed with austere landscapes of São Paulo and vulnerable self-portraits Fajardo made while hospitalized. “From the perspective of a powerless close witness, this book shows a side of pregnancy that is not usually seen,” notes Linneu. “One that, despite being painful and dark, is still beautiful, powerful, and meaningful.” Printed mostly in black and white on deckle-edged paper, the book has a heft and rawness befitting both its subject matter and Linneu’s candid, deeply personal approach. Valentín, now eleven, drew the cover of JJ VFF VV , a book that shows the complex layers of joy, pain, and uncertainty that accompany the creation of a family.

blocks.caption: Yufan Lu, Inside a waiting room in a cosmetic surgery clinic in Beijing, China , from Make Me Beautiful , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Make Me Beautiful by Yufan Lu Editorial RM, México and Barcelona; Ediciones Posibles and Fundación Photographic Social Vision, Barcelona; Phree, Madrid. Design by Min Lyu

Yufan Lu’s Make Me Beautiful is an intrepid exploration and critique of the beauty standards and societal expectations imposed on women in China. In an attempt to understand a complex and burgeoning industry, Lu visited over thirty cosmetic surgery clinics with her own self-portrait. Sterile interiors of the clinics are paired with iterations of facial maps and diagnoses received from “beauty designers,” alongside their transcribed medical advice. Throughout this minimally designed book—reinforced with a pale pink, gauze-like fabric on the spine—Lu places the industry under a microscope. By inserting screenshots from social media, cutouts, and collages using presurgery portraits of women, she offers a clever and impactful perspective on the endless expectations in the name of beauty.

blocks.caption: Swan Moon, from Swan Moon’s Swan Moon , 2025 Courtesy of TBW Books

blocks.text: Swan Moon’s Swan Moon by Swan Moon TBW Books, Oakland, California. Design by Paul Schiek

Swan Moon is a diaristic chronicle of the photographer Swan Moon’s experience growing up as a Korean American in Los Angeles. In the 1990s, inspired by the cinematic mythology of her environment, a teenaged Moon and her friends played pretend, blending everyday snapshots with staged scenes featuring clothing and props gleaned from vintage shops. Her black-and-white photographs channel, through their own lo-fi scrappiness, the noir glamour of Hollywood, which is also reflected in the book’s design, featuring dramatic blackout pages that lend the images a silver-screen quality. The result is a beguiling meditation on youth, the make believe of identity, and the lures of nostalgia.

blocks.caption: Peter Rauch, Bones (0104) , 2024 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: 2, 3 by Peter Rauch Perimeter Editions, Melbourne. Design by Žiga Testen

When a building is structurally sound, a realtor might say it has “good bones.” Peter Rauch, an architect and photographer, takes this adage literally in 2, 3 , a survey of ten years of precise but enigmatic photography, performance, installation, and theoretical inquiry into the infrastructure of small buildings and human bodies. Raush grew up in Ljubljana, Slovenia, in the 1980s, in that “crack” in time “between late socialism and late capitalism,” Žiga Testen writes in 2, 3 , a softcover photobook with glossy pages like a magazine or catalog. While his evenly lit images of mundane buildings and interiors in states of construction or disarray resemble Thomas Ruff’s late-1970s deadpan scenes of Düsseldorf, Rauch’s forensic pictures of bone fragments and construction materials look like official documentation for a science museum. Raush frequently pulls back the frame, showing pictures of his own pictures and installation views of his exhibitions, self-reflexively “polishing the edges,” Testen observes, as “views turn into objects, objects into images, and back again.”

blocks.caption: Allie Tsubota, Ōta River Park, Hiroshima , from Dead Letter Room , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Dead Letter Room: A Transhistorical Correspondence with Hara Tamiki by Allie Tsubota The Eriskay Connection, Breda, Netherlands. Design by Carel Fransen

links.text: Dead Letter Room: A Transhistorical Correspondence with Hara Tamiki

blocks.text: Dead Letter Room is a transhistorical correspondence with Japanese poet and survivor of the bombing of Hiroshima, Hara Tamiki (1905–1951). This delicate, slender volume begins with a visual archive of the United States Strategic Bombing Survey (USSBS)—footage produced by the US military in occupied Japan in 1945—presented as a beautifully rendered sequence of lithographs. A series of imagined letters between Tsubota and Hara center the book, composing a cross-generational dialogue that chronicles an exploration of memory, loss, and history. Tsubota’s own photographs, made in Tokyo and Hiroshima in 2022 and punctuated by Hara’s writing, investigate the impact of the war on the contemporary landscape.

blocks.caption: Joël van Houdt, Kabul , October 2010, from Afghanistanism , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Afghanistanism by Joël van Houdt Self-published, London. Design by -SYB-

The term Afghanistanism , coined in the 1950s by Western journalists and politicians, is defined as the practice of focusing on problems in distant parts of the world while ignoring controversial local issues. Dutch photographer Joël van Houdt’s self-published debut brings together a collection of photographs made between 2010 and 2022 with quotes from people visiting Afghanistan over the last two centuries. The project explores the boundaries of the outsider’s gaze, drawing a parallel between an occupying army enforcing a way of life and a photographer striving to understand it. “I watched as life continued with resilience and courage but also with creativity and humor,” van Houdt notes in his postscript, “in defiance of all that opposed it.”

blocks.caption: Farren van Wyk, Boycott Outspan Oranges , 2023, from Mixedness Is My Mythology , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Mixedness Is My Mythology by Farren van Wyk Fw:Books, Amsterdam, and Deadbeat Club, Los Angeles. Design by Hans Gremmen

Mixedness Is My Mythology navigates what it means to exist between cultures and communities. Born in South Africa in 1993, the last year of apartheid, before moving to the Netherlands at age six, Farren van Wyk uses portraiture to consider her intersectional heritage. Photographing herself and her family on their Dutch family farm, van Wyk subverts aesthetics from archival colonial photography to challenge perceptions of race and singular identity. The black-and-white images are richly printed on uncoated paper, and occasional inserts of metallic silver pages suggest how the work might serve as a mirror to lived experience.
PhotoBook of the Year

blocks.caption: Michele Borzoni and Rocco Rorandelli, from Silent Springs , 2026 © the artists and courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Silent Springs by Michele Borzoni and Rocco Rorandelli Loose Joints Publishing, Marseille, France / London. Design by Tommaso Tanini

Italian photographic duo Michele Borzoni and Rocco Rorandelli’s Silent Springs follows climate activism across Europe, documenting the nonviolent direct action of several climate justice movements. Dubbed “an official glossary of climate activism,” this substantial paperback traces the various stages of activism, providing the reader with accessible language on civil disobedience alongside photographs that reveal the discipline and organization of the movements to form a contemporary manifesto of the infrastructure of resistance. With its title adopted from Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring , the influential 1962 book about the harms of pesticides, Borzoni and Rorandelli’s timely investigation reveals how resistance is learned and sustained within communities.

blocks.caption: Bieke Depoorter, Russia , January 11, 2009 , from The Beds I Slept In , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: The Beds I Slept In by Bieke Depoorter Hannibal Books, Antwerp, Belgium. Design by Armand Mevis and Bieke Depoorter

Because she was a young woman, and a foreigner, people told the Belgian photographer Bieke Depoorter that what she was doing was dangerous: asking strangers to spend a night in their homes. Yet, when she looked back at her archives from travels between 2008 and 2016 to Egypt, Russia, and the US, she found hundreds of seemingly casual pictures of the beds she had slept in and wondered, she says, if she had been “collecting evidence.” In The Beds I Slept In , sized like a travel guide, complete with a Swiss-style open binding that resembles a stack of sheets, Depoorter divides these images into three regions, tracing journeys on the Trans-Siberian Railway or from Seattle to New York or around Cairo, and adding observations both banal (“Not sure what I am doing”) and world historical (“Osama bin Laden killed”). People and animals sometimes appear, but it’s the emptiness of beds that creates a sense of pathos and self-reflection—and the random signs that could be taken as koans, like a painting that reads: “She believed she could, so she did.”

blocks.caption: Bérangère Fromont, from République , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: République by Bérangère Fromont Chose Commune, Marseille, France. Design by Cécile Poimbœuf-Koizumi and Perrine Serre

In 2023, Bérangère Fromont began photographing at the Place de la République in Paris, a site famous for political gatherings and protests from the 1800s to today. In République , Fromont trains her lens on the young generations who frequent the space, conveying the subtle daily shifts between calm and resistance, collective and individual. Photographing in black and white, Fromont’s chiaroscuro-esque frames narrow in on the details of gesture and emotion: a scrunched-up face in contemplation; protestors in states of rest; individualistic elements of style and dress. The book’s minimal design and softcover binding pair elegantly with Fromont’s tightly cropped photographs to form an intimate yet fragmented picture of a generation marked by uncertainty about the future and a turbulent political environment.

blocks.caption: Roger Grasas, from WALLS: A Visual Study on Border Geographies , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: WALLS: A Visual Study on Border Geographies by Roger Grasas Institut de les Desigualtats, Barcelona. Design by Studio Carles Murillo

links.text: WALLS: A Visual Study on Border Geographies

blocks.text: The notion of the border originated alongside the earliest civilizations as a humanmade boundary designed to safeguard land and resources. Roger Grasas’s WALLS: A Visual Study on Border Geographies interrogates the concept of the border not just as an imaginary line but as a mechanism of exclusion, control, and separation. Substantial in both physical size and investigative depth, this encyclopedic photobook spans geographies, testimonies, and case studies across four continents, documenting lived experiences of those encountered along the way. As Grasas states in the book’s introduction, “ WALLS confronts us with the world we are building and with the gaze through which we choose—or refuse—to recognize the ‘face’ of alterity.”

blocks.caption: Nick Haymes, from Chronograph , 2026

blocks.text: Chronograph by Nick Haymes SPBH Editions, London. Design by Lina Kutsovskaya and Brian Paul Lamotte

Family can be “a lot,” so why not use a lot of pictures to describe the endlessly rich universe of family dynamics? Chronograph includes more than one thousand photographs that Nick Haymes made over a quarter of a century, shifting seamlessly between color and black and white, to chronicle the beauty and unvarnished chaos of family life as time inexorably marches along. With full bleeds as well as grids of multiple images, the book bursts with the anarchic energy of childhood, sibling interplay, daily rituals, the physical transformations of puberty, and gleeful family adventures on the road. At the book’s start, jarring images of the Twin Towers aflame on 9/11, made in the early days of Haymes’s relationship with his partner, Lina, are a reminder of life’s fragility in an unpredictable world.

blocks.caption: Takashi Homma, from This Is Not My Cat , 2025 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: This Is Not My Cat by Takashi Homma Nieves, Zurich, and Perimeter Editions, Melbourne. Design by Benjamin Sommerhalder

There is an argument to be made that cats are a photographer’s best friend. Both are inquisitive, strongly independent beings fond of roaming about and obsessively observing. With its small, chapbook-like format and restrained edit, This Is Not My Cat makes the case that bigger is not better and that the simplest idea is often the strongest one. Here, a modest form elegantly serves a photographer’s ode to his cat that is also a tribute to the profound connections between people and their pets. A memorable addition to the growing pantheon of feline-centric photography books.

blocks.caption: Sohrab Hura, from Snow , 2026 Courtesy the artist and MACK

blocks.text: Snow by Sohrab Hura MACK, London. Design by Sohrab Hura

From 2014 to 2019, Sohrab Hura made dozens of trips to the disputed Himalayan territory of Kashmir, over which India now exercises ironclad control. Snow , the resulting (and ongoing) series, contrasts the region’s militarization with its perception as a paradise for tourists, particularly Indian visitors drawn by its snowfall. Bound in tactile, image-printed linen, this book is an oblique meditation on conflict, its baggy edit of 175 images forming an enveloping, open-ended narrative that rejects photojournalistic spectacle for an atmospheric view of everyday life in Kashmir. In the beautiful, blinding nature of snow, Hura locates a compelling metaphor for the ways landscapes of violence are both seen and obscured.

blocks.caption: Zhu Mo, Undercurrents , 2020 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Undercurrents by Zhu Mo JZZP, Ningbo, China. Design by PAY2PLAY

In 2014, photographer Zhu Mo left Beijing and traveled along China’s national highways, photographing cities, people, and landscapes he encountered during his journey. The nine-year project became Undercurrents , a book beautifully structured to mimic his aimlessness. Printed as individual, loose-leaf sheets, the color images can be freely removed and rearranged, challenging the conventions of a traditional narrative sequence. At nearly four hundred pages—each numbered in a vibrant blue—the capacious book features rough-cut edges, blank pages, and shifting photographs that invite the reader to take on the active role of an editor.

blocks.caption: Keisha Scarville, from Passports , 2026 Courtesy the artist and MACK

blocks.text: Passports 2012–2025 by Keisha Scarville MACK, London. Design by Keisha Scarville and Morgan Crowcroft-Brown

Since 2012, Keisha Scarville has been reworking an ID photo from her father’s first passport, taken when he was sixteen years old and living in Guyana. She has embellished each reproduction of the photo with daubs of paint or little beads or collaged images from magazines, amassing a collection of three hundred unique artworks. Sometimes her father has red skin; sometimes he’s surrounded by black stars. Tears of yellow ribbons fall from his eyes, or abstract masks obscure his face altogether. The tactile variations layered over the ID photo causes “an irrepressible urge to touch,” writes Tina M. Campt in Passports , a book that meditates on the love between a father and a daughter, and the ambiguous relationship between homeland and diaspora. Scaled to the size of a novel and studded with ruminative lines from a dialogue with Scarville’s father, Passports , which gestures to the collages and painterly techniques of Lorna Simpson, Chris Ofili, and Kerry James Marshall, is an indelible photo-essay about the meaning of kinship.

blocks.caption: Newsha Tavakolian, 09_Tehran, 2017 , from And They Laughed at Me , 2026 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: And They Laughed at Me by Newsha Tavakolian Kehrer Verlag, Heidelberg, Germany. Design by Kehrer Design, Laura Pecoroni

In And They Laughed at Me , Newsha Tavakolian revisits her archive, drawing together what she refers to as “eyesore” photographs to highlight two decades of her early practice as a photojournalist in her native Tehran. Tavakolian embraces the imperfections of these images: contact sheets run across spreads; light leaks, taped together images, and scratches are left in; negatives run fully, whether half-broken or with the full rough borders. The book’s dust jacket unfurls into a double-sided poster, and inside, handwritten notes from Tavakolian peppered throughout the pages provide short details for the events she depicts. And They Laughed at Me is a propulsive, unvarnished portrait of memory, politics, and artistic growth.
Photography Catalog of the Year

blocks.caption: Dimakatso Mathopa, Individual Beings (Moving VI) , 2024 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: A Kind of Paradise: Artistic Counter-Narratives to Colonial-Era Photography , Edited by Nanina Guyer Spector Books, Leipzig, Germany. Design by NODE Berlin Oslo

links.text: A Kind of Paradise: Artistic Counter-Narratives to Colonial-Era Photography

blocks.text: The nineteenth century haunts this book like a ghost in the attic. Photography’s first decades of innovation, beginning in the 1840s, coincided with European colonial expansion around the world, and the reduction—through images—of indigenous populations to seemingly exotic strangers and spectacles. Countless subjects of imperial photographers remain in archives as unnamed, misunderstood “examples” supposedly meant to prove a misbegotten idea about cultural inferiority. But can nineteenth-century photographs also become a space of reinvention? This question is at the heart of A Kind of Paradise , which surveys a generation of artists using memory as material. Cleverly, the book opens in the present, with interventions into archives through wide-ranging acts of appropriation, collage, and performance, gradually introducing the voices of leading scholars on postcolonial visual history. “Even in photography’s darkest moments,” the curator Nanina Guyer writes, “redemption is possible—when revelation becomes protection, and the archive itself becomes an act of love.”

blocks.caption: Julián Barón, El laberinto mágico , 2019 Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Ecos de la Memoria (Echoes of Memory) , Edited by Marta Martín Núñez Editorial RM, Mexico City and Barcelona, and Campgràfic Editors, Valencia, Spain. Design by Underbau

links.text: Ecos de la Memoria (Echoes of Memory)

blocks.text: Surveying more than 120 photobooks and catalogs, Echoes of Memory explores how later generations have grappled with the legacy of the Spanish Civil War and Francisco Franco’s dictatorship, a subject shaped by decades of political silence and competing efforts to reckon with the past. This weighty theme is organized into a bold yet unobtrusive design whose neutral gray cover reflects a restrained approach to contested history, while its showiest feature—a detachable timeline cover—offers a tangible framework for situating fragmentary images and narratives within the chronology of the war. Rather than advance an “official” history, this vital bilingual compendium reveals how gaps and unresolved histories continue to shape how national trauma is passed from one generation to the next.

blocks.caption: Carlos Idun-Tawiah, Many Reasons to Live Again , 2022 Courtesy the artist and Galleria Alta

blocks.text: Ghana! Rêver l’indépendance, 1957–1976 , Edited by Damarice Amao Atelier EXB, Paris. Design by Line Célo

When Ghana declared independence from British colonial rule on March 6, 1957, a new nation was born, one that needed to project itself onto the global stage with a spirit of optimism. The following decade would see the proliferation of photobooks, government publications, and news magazines extolling Ghana’s infrastructure, healthcare, hydroelectric power, and cultural prowess. Published to accompany an exhibition at Les Rencontres d’Arles, this vivacious catalog surveys the photographic culture of Ghana’s postindependence years, showing how Ghanaians wanted their lives and aspirations portrayed, from the magazine page to the portrait studio. Rooted in selections from James Barnor’s radiant 1950s portraiture and Paul Strand’s stately Ghana: An African Portrait (1976), Ghana! brings readers up to the present with recent color photography by Carlos Idun-Tawiah, who shows through his homage to Barnor the sartorial value and social memory to be mined from nostalgia.

blocks.caption: Adam Broomberg and Oliver Chanarin, “P is for Painting” (“P comme Peindre”), Humans and Other Animals (Humains et autres animaux) , Tate Publishing, London, 2015 © Late Estate of Broomberg and Chanarin

blocks.text: L Is for Look: Children’s Photobooks , Edited by Anne Lacoste and Rose Durr Spector Books, Leipzig, Germany. Design by Ina Kwon and Helmut Völter

links.text: L Is for Look: Children’s Photobooks

blocks.text: L is for Look illuminates the vibrant but previously underexplored field of children’s photobooks. Featuring more than one hundred global examples, from the 1930s through the present, this catalog is organized thematically by editorial approach and concept: the pedagogical, designed to instruct toddlers on vocabulary or the alphabet or promote an understanding of geometric shapes and forms; fictional storytelling paired with photographs, creating tensions between invented narratives and depictions of reality; animals, often anthropomorphized and conversing; and “photographism,” the interaction of photography, graphic design, and other media. The books assembled here no doubt captured the imaginations of young people when they were first published, just as this compendium, with its delightful array of visual pleasures—and rich contextual research—will be equally illuminating for readers of all ages today.

blocks.caption: Blommers & Schumm, The Class of 1998 for Self Service , 1998

blocks.text: More , Edited by Anuschka Blommers, Niels Schumm, and Julie Peeters Blommers & Schumm, Roma Publications, Amsterdam. Design by Julie Peeters

Since the late 1990s, Blommers and Schumm have brought a distinct form of highly constructed, intriguingly odd imagery to the space of fashion. Their output runs the gamut, encompassing deadpan portraiture, forensically precise still lifes, and seductively awkward choreography. More , released in parallel with a survey exhibition at FOAM, Amsterdam, collects twenty-five years of work, some made for magazines such as Self Service , The Gentlewoman , Fantastic Man , Interview , and Purple , revealing how the editorial page remains a blank canvas for experimentation and a venue to play with traditional ideas of what constitutes a fashion picture. Oversized and softcover, with the appropriate feel of a magazine, the book’s cover features an extreme close-up of ants exploring a lush, pink flower, alerting viewers to the colliding forces of beauty and the uncanny inside the book.
Contributions by Brendan Embser, Michael Famighetti, Daniela Grande, Zack Hatfield, Sofia Headley, Noa Lin, Cassidy Paul, Alex Schlechter, and Gia Sidhu.
